title: SYSK Selects: How Police Chases Work
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the 2013 episode on police chases. Josh and Chuck cover how little training officers get for high-speed pursuit (about two days, with Colorado State Police's Emergency Vehicles Operation course as the standout), how police cruisers are equipped differently (Crown Victoria fuel-fire issues, heavier duty cooling, alternators, vinyl rear seats, light bars), and tools for ending chases such as spike strips, roadblocks, the PIT maneuver, and laser/microwave technologies like StarChase. They discuss the danger to bystanders, the fact that most chases are for non-violent offenses, department pursuit policies (Washington D.C., Des Moines, Orlando), legal protections like sovereign immunity, and how TV chase shows present a one-sided picture.

segments.title: Rerun intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the SYSK Selects episode on police chases, originally released May 2013, and the hosts riff on British sirens and the show's law enforcement series.

segments.title: Danger of police chases and police driver training
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the deaths of about 140 innocent bystanders a year in chases, and how police get only about a week of driver training, with about two days on high-speed pursuit. They describe the Colorado State Police Emergency Vehicles Operation course as a top program.

segments.title: Police cruiser equipment and the Crown Victoria
segments.summary: The Ford Crown Victoria is discussed as the most common police car, along with its fuel-fire problems compared to the Pinto and the chemical fire suppression system. Police cars get more horsepower, reinforced seat backs, extra coolers, bigger alternators, vinyl rear seats, and light bars from the 1970s.

segments.title: Tools for stopping a chase
segments.summary: Methods to end pursuits are covered: spike strips, roadblocks (with the risk of funneling suspects into neighborhoods), the PIT maneuver, and modern laser and microwave technologies such as StarChase that disable a vehicle fitted with a special microchip.

segments.title: Deciding whether to pursue and supervisor role
segments.summary: Officers run plates and weigh the offense, with the violent-criminal case as the most widely supported reason to chase. Most chases involve non-violent offenses (91.4 percent per the hosts). Supervisors are expected to keep a cool head and may call off pursuits, relying on helicopters.

segments.title: Chase TV shows, legal protections, and closing
segments.summary: Hosts critique TV chase shows like Cops for a one-sided view of pursuits and discuss local policies such as Washington D.C., Des Moines, and Orlando rules, plus sovereign immunity and liability. The episode closes with a call for reviews and the Kiva team.
